topic.name: Finding Trigonometric Ratios of Special Angles Using the Unit Circle

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ corresponds to the point $\left( -\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin\left( \dfrac {2\pi} {3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}.$

example.title: Finding the Sine or Cosine of a Special Angle Given in Radians

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$ corresponds to the point $\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \right).$

  • Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos\left( \dfrac {5\pi} {4}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}.$

  • Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin\left( \dfrac {5\pi} {4}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\tan{\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},$ we have

\[ \tan\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sin{\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) }}{\cos{\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) }} = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right)}{\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt 2} {2}\right)} = 1. \]
